description:
We are AstroBai, a team of passionate students from Valencia City, Bukidnon, combining our love for technology, space exploration, and innovation. Our name blends "Astronaut" and "Bai," a Bisaya term for bro! 

We're developing an interactive STEM game that makes space exploration fun and educational. We welcome creative minds with skills in game development, programming, UI/UX design, digital art, and scientific research. Join us as we explore beyond Earth!
summary: AstroBai: Red Frontier is a browser-based Mars outpost game for children ages 7–12. Players take care of a small crew, decide where to send power, and investigate a bright clue beneath the Martian dust through Project ICEBOUND. Across five story chapters and a planned ten-sol mission, players face choices about repairs, shelter, and how to collect and study a sample. The game makes trade-offs visible through a pixel-art outpost, short conversations, and feedback that explains why things change. Its goal is to help young players understand how space crews make decisions with limited supplies and why an uncertain or negative result can still teach scientists something.
details:
AstroBai: Red Frontier is a browser-based Mars outpost game designed for children ages 7–12. The player helps a small crew prepare for launch, travel to Mars, and run an outpost. The mission design groups ten Martian days, called sols, into five story chapters. Each chapter gives the player a clear goal and a decision they can discuss afterward, such as repairing damaged equipment, choosing how to investigate a possible ice deposit, or sheltering during a solar storm.

The outpost is the main place to play. Children can select the Habitat, Solar Array, Greenhouse, and Research Laboratory, watch an astronaut walk to the selected building, and enter illustrated rooms to inspect equipment. Looking around is free. The dashboard shows Energy, Oxygen, Food, and Water with icons, words, and color. Quick Plan cards let players compare ways to share power. An optional Engineer’s Panel opens five sliders for players who want to examine each allocation. A child can start with a simple choice and explore the numbers when they’re curious.

Our creative approach is to make a decision visible in the world where it happens. A damaged Solar Array looks different from a working one. A shelter warning changes how the crew is shown. Through Project ICEBOUND, the same map becomes a place to investigate a clue. Players compare sending a rover, an astronaut, or both. The discovery screen shows which clues contributed to the sample result. It treats positive, inconclusive, and negative results as opportunities to learn. The debrief then asks players to reflect on a decision and consider what they would try on another mission.

We wanted children to practice explaining why they made a choice. For example, if they give more power to the laboratory, what might have to wait elsewhere? We designed short dialogue, one clear goal at a time, optional science explanations, and a gentle tone when a mission needs another try. We also considered keyboard access, visible focus, readable controls on smaller screens, reduced motion, and how to communicate warnings without relying on color alone.

We built AstroBai with React, TypeScript, Vite, CSS, and SVG. We used Git and GitHub for team development and Vercel for web deployment. The prototype demonstrates the story screens, interactive outpost, facility interiors, Power Plan controls, mission choices, discovery screen, and debrief. Several screens use preview data while the team connects the full simulation and shared game state.
